definitions.definition: Awareness: the knowing, luminous nature of mind recognized as the ground itself — empty, clear, unobstructed and unfabricated. It is distinguished from ordinary mind (sems), which grasps at objects; recognizing rig pa through the master's introduction is the entry to the Great Perfection.
In the Nyingma generally, the awareness that is the fruit of the inner tantras and the object of the introduction; 'awareness-holder' (rig 'dzin, vidyādhara) names those who hold it.
In Bön Dzogchen, awareness inseparable from the base of all (kun gzhi); their union is the natural state.

cross_language.note: translation equivalent; the Sanskrit word has other senses in other traditions

equivalents.note: Mipham identifies buddha-nature as luminosity-emptiness, the nature Dzogchen introduces as rig pa

definitions.definition: Ordinary mind: the dualistic, conceptual consciousness that grasps subject and object and arises from not recognizing the ground; to be distinguished from awareness (rig pa). In the Kunjed Gyalpo, however, 'sems' in byang chub sems names the all-creating nature itself.
The moving mind distinguished from the nature of mind (sems nyid) in Bön Dzogchen.

Ignorance as non-recognition of the ground-appearances as one's own display; in three kinds: the ignorance of single identity (bdag nyid gcig pu), co-emergent ignorance (lhan cig skyes pa) and conceptualizing ignorance (kun tu brtags pa). From it dualistic grasping and saṃsāra unfold.
In the Guhyagarbha, the conceptuality by which beings, of one nature with the buddhas, grasp 'I' and 'mine' and wander in the five classes.

equivalents.note: Dzogchen's non-recognition of the ground is the root the Abhidharma lists as the first link; the Dzogchen account adds its genesis from the ground-appearances

definitions.definition: The ground: the primordial state of all beings and phenomena prior to saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, whose essence is primordially pure, nature spontaneously present and compassion all-pervading; recognized it is buddhahood, unrecognized it is the basis of delusion.
In the ground-path-fruit scheme of the Nyingma tantras, the ground is the buddha-nature present in beings, the path its recognition and cultivation, the fruit its manifestation.

cross_language.note: loose equivalent; the Dzogchen sense has no exact Sanskrit counterpart recorded

definitions.definition: Primordial purity: the empty essence of the ground, pure from the beginning ('ka', the first letter), never stained by delusion; realized through cutting through (khregs chod).
Spontaneous presence: the luminous nature of the ground, in which all qualities, lights and kāyas are present without being produced; brought to manifestation in direct crossing (thod rgal).
In Mahāyoga, the spontaneously present maṇḍala of deities (lhun grub kyi dkyil 'khor).
Essence: the first of the three aspects of the ground — empty, primordially pure.

cross_language.note: in other contexts ngo bo translates svabhāva / bhāva

definitions.definition: Nature: the second aspect of the ground — luminous, spontaneously present.
Compassion or responsiveness: the third aspect of the ground — its unceasing, all-pervading capacity to manifest, the source of the ground-appearances.
Compassion (karuṇā) as the motivation of the path and the activity of the buddhas.

The all-base: in Longchenpa's usage the neutral, unaware basis in which karmic tendencies are stored, the root of saṃsāra; it must be distinguished from the dharmakāya — to rest in it is not to rest in awareness.
The base of all: in Bön Dzogchen the ultimate ground, empty and clear, inseparable from awareness; not the saṃsāric storehouse.

equivalents.note: the Nyingma distinguish the all-base (kun gzhi) from the all-base consciousness (kun gzhi rnam shes); both belong to the saṃsāric side
Bön's kun gzhi functions as the ground (gzhi) of Nyingma Dzogchen, while the Nyingma kun gzhi does not

notes: The same Tibetan word names different doctrines in Nyingma and Bön usage; do not merge the definitions.

definitions.definition: Ground-appearances: the display that arises from the ground when its compassion stirs, through the eight gateways of spontaneous presence; recognized as self-display they are liberation (Samantabhadra), not recognized they become the basis of delusion.
Self-arising wisdom: the all-creating king's own name for itself in the Kunjed Gyalpo — wisdom without causes and conditions, beyond effort, unobscured.
The youthful vase body: the ground's luminosity enclosed within, like a lamp in a vase, not yet radiating outward; when the 'seal' of the vase breaks, the ground-appearances arise.
Expressive power: the ground's capacity to manifest; with 'radiance' (gdangs) and 'display' (rol pa) one of the three modes in which energy appears.
Display or play: appearances arising as the ground's self-display, like reflections in a crystal.
Uncontrived, unaltered: awareness left as it is, without correction or fabrication; 'let no one alter this' (Kunjed Gyalpo ch.32).
Leaving as it is: the four ways of leaving things as they are (view like a mountain, meditation like an ocean, conduct as appearances, fruit as awareness).

Self-liberation: thoughts and appearances liberate by themselves when recognized in awareness, without an antidote; with primordial liberation (ye grol), liberation on arising (shar grol), naked liberation (cer grol) and liberation from extremes (mtha' grol) it forms the modes of liberation.
Liberation upon arising: a thought is freed in the very moment it arises, like a drawing on water.
Unobstructed, transparent, all-penetrating: a quality of awareness and the name of Rigdzin Gödem's treasure (Gongpa Zangthal).
Direct introduction: the master's pointing out of awareness to the disciple, the first of Garab Dorje's three statements.
The introduction to the natural state in the Zhang Zhung Nyengyü.
The empowerment of the expressive power of awareness: the Dzogchen empowerment that introduces awareness, beyond the four empowerments of the lower tantras.

Meditative experiences — above all bliss, clarity and non-thought — which are signs of practice but, if grasped, lead into the desire, form and formless realms; they are transient, unlike realization (rtogs pa).

Cutting through (literally 'cutting tightness'): the Great Perfection practice of recognizing primordially pure awareness and resting in it so that thoughts self-liberate; taught before direct crossing.

Direct crossing (literally 'leap over'): the instruction-series practice in which spontaneous presence manifests through the four visions, culminating in the exhaustion of phenomena and, for some, the rainbow body. Restricted: taught only orally to those stable in cutting through.

The four visions of direct crossing: the direct perception of dharmatā (chos nyid mngon sum), the increase of experience (nyams gong 'phel), awareness reaching its full measure (rig pa tshad phebs), and the exhaustion of phenomena in dharmatā (chos nyid du zad pa).

Rainbow body: the fruit in which the body's gross elements dissolve into their essence of light at death, leaving only hair and nails (or nothing); the 'great transference' ('pho ba chen po) body of Padmasambhava and Vimalamitra departs without death.
The rainbow body attained by masters of the Zhang Zhung Nyengyü and, by Bön tradition, by Shardza Tashi Gyaltsen.

(1) A practitioner's meditative commitment or daily practice; (2) the state in which an accomplished practitioner remains in the clear light after the breath has stopped, the body staying lifelike and warm at the heart for days.

literal: dividing the boundary of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa

definitions.definition: Separating saṃsāra and nirvāṇa: the extraordinary preliminaries of the Heart-essence (outer, inner, secret) that distinguish ordinary mind from awareness.
'Holding the mind': a set of Heart-essence exercises (traditionally twenty-one) using postures, sounds, breath and visualization to bring about experiences in which awareness can be recognized.

notes: The number twenty-one and the attribution to the Tegchok Dzöd are from memory.

definitions.definition: The preliminaries: the common outer preliminaries (the four thoughts that turn the mind, with the benefits of liberation and following a teacher) and the uncommon inner preliminaries (refuge with prostration, bodhicitta, Vajrasattva, maṇḍala, kusāli, guru yoga), each traditionally accumulated a hundred thousand times.
Bön preliminaries parallel in structure (refuge, bodhicitta, purification, maṇḍala, guru yoga with Tapihritsa or Shenrab).
The three roots: the guru (root of blessing), the yidam (root of accomplishment) and the ḍākinī or protector (root of activity) — the inner refuge of Vajrayāna.
The meditational deity with whom one's mind is bound by samaya; the root of accomplishment, practised in the generation and completion stages.
Channels and winds: the completion-stage yogas working with the subtle body (channels, winds, essences), emphasized in Anuyoga; restricted practices taught under guidance.
The Bön practices of channels and winds from the Mother Tantra and the Zhang Zhung Nyengyü.
'Magical wheel': sequences of physical movement combined with breath holding, practised with the completion stage and in Dzogchen retreats (restricted).
The trulkhor of the Zhang Zhung Nyengyü (restricted).

Transference of consciousness at death to a pure land or to the dharmakāya; five kinds are distinguished (dharmakāya, sambhogakāya, nirmāṇakāya, ordinary, and the transference for the dead by compassion). Restricted: never applied before the time.

Intermediate state: any interval between two states — six bardos (of life, dream, meditation, dying, dharmatā and becoming), or four in the Heart-essence (natural bardo of life, of dying, of dharmatā, of becoming).

equivalents.note: the bardo of becoming is the Abhidharma's intermediate existence; the Nyingma extend 'bardo' to every intermediate state

definitions.definition: Clear light, luminosity: the nature of mind manifest at death (the ground or mother luminosity), in deep sleep and in meditation (the path or child luminosity); their meeting at death is liberation.

equivalents.note: the Nyingma's clear light at death is the naturally luminous mind of the sūtras manifest

definitions.definition: The seventh vehicle, first of the inner tantras: emphasis on the generation stage and on the view that all phenomena are the great purity and equality of the deities; its tantras divide into a tantra section (the eighteen tantras, chief the Guhyagarbha) and a sādhana section (the Eight Herukas).

notes: Homonym of the haṭha 'mahāyoga' (trm:mahayoga), with a different meaning; kept separate.

definitions.definition: The eighth vehicle: emphasis on the completion stage (channels, winds and essences) and on the inseparability of expanse and wisdom; its root scripture is the Dupa Do.

notes: Homonym of the Jain 'anuyoga' (trm:anuyoga, exposition); kept separate.

definitions.definition: The ninth and highest vehicle, the Great Perfection: emphasis on awareness itself, beyond generation and completion.
'Utmost yoga' (shin tu rnal 'byor): the Kunjed Gyalpo's name for the yogin who is the all-creator.
The Great Perfection: the teaching that everything is complete (rdzogs) in the nature of mind and that there is nothing beyond it (chen po); also the name of the ninth vehicle.
The unsurpassed way (bla med) of Bön, taught in the A-tri, the Dzogchen Yangtse Longchen and the Zhang Zhung Nyengyü.

The mind series: the first of the three series of Dzogchen, teaching that all appearances are the display of mind-nature (bodhicitta); root texts the Kunjed Gyalpo and the eighteen mind-series scriptures.
The space series: the second series, teaching that everything is self-liberated in the vast expanse (klong), transmitted chiefly through Vairocana.

The instruction series: the third series, of pith instructions, in four cycles (outer, inner, secret, innermost secret); the innermost secret cycle is the Heart-essence with cutting through and direct crossing.
Heart-essence: the innermost secret unsurpassed cycle of the instruction series (Vima Nyingthig, Khandro Nyingthig, Longchen Nyingthig).
The nine vehicles: śrāvaka, pratyekabuddha, bodhisattva; kriyā, ubhaya (caryā), yoga; mahāyoga, anuyoga, atiyoga.
The nine ways of Bön: four causal and five fruitional ways.

Great purity and equality: the Mahāyoga view that all phenomena are primordially pure as the deities and pure lands (relative) and equal in emptiness (ultimate), inseparable — the 'superior two truths'.

The Eight Pronouncements / Eight Herukas of the Mahāyoga sādhana section: Mañjuśrī-Yamāntaka (body), Hayagrīva (speech), Yangdag (mind), Chemchok / Amṛta (qualities), Vajrakīla (activity), Mamo (sending and calling the mātaraḥ), Jigten Chötö (worldly offering and praise) and Möpa Drakngak (wrathful mantra).
The 'spoken word': the long lineage of scriptures and instructions transmitted without interruption from master to disciple since the first diffusion.

Treasure: teachings, objects or substances concealed (chiefly by Padmasambhava and Yeshe Tsogyal) in the earth, rocks, water, sky or the minds of disciples, to be revealed at the destined time by a treasure revealer — the 'short lineage'.
Bön treasures concealed during the persecutions and recovered from the 10th-11th c. (Shenchen Luga).
Treasure revealer: a person prophesied and empowered in a former life (usually as a disciple of Padmasambhava) to reveal treasures; the 'five kings' and many others.
Mind treasure: a teaching concealed in the revealer's mind-stream and arising from it at the right time (e.g. the Longchen Nyingthig).
Earth treasure: a treasure recovered from a physical place (rock, lake, temple pillar), often a scroll in symbolic script that triggers the teaching.
Ḍākinī symbolic script: the coded letters on treasure scrolls which only the destined revealer can decode.
Inventory or certificate: a guide text indicating the place and content of a treasure.
Treasure protector: the guardian spirit or deity entrusted with a treasure until its revealer comes.
Re-concealed treasure: a treasure revealed, hidden again and revealed a second time.
Pure vision: a teaching received directly from a buddha or master in a vision — the 'profound' third lineage beside kama and terma.
Emanation body (nirmāṇakāya); in Tibetan usage also a recognized reincarnation of a master, a system in which many Nyingma treasure revealers and abbots are identified.

A lay (non-celibate) tantric practitioner, often a householder of a hereditary lineage, wearing white robes and long hair: the 'white-robed, long-haired community' (gos dkar lcang lo'i sde) of the Nyingma.
Gathering circle (gaṇacakra): a feast offering to the deities, the lineage and the guests, with confession and restoration of samaya.
Ritual cake (bali) offered to deities, protectors and spirits, or used as a support of the deity.
Accomplishment of sacred medicine: the great-accomplishment ritual in which consecrated pills (dam rdzas) are prepared through days of collective sādhana.
Great accomplishment: an intensive collective sādhana performed continuously for several days, often combined with medicine accomplishment.
The purification rite for the dead, performed with the deceased's name card (byang bu) and the peaceful and wrathful deities, to purify obscurations and guide the consciousness.
Signs of death: outer (bodily), inner (breath) and secret (dream) signs that death is approaching.
Ransoming or cheating death: rites (such as saving the lives of animals and offering effigies) performed when signs of untimely death appear.

Lamp: in the instruction series, the channels and faculties through which awareness manifests — counted as four lamps (the far-reaching water lamp, the lamp of the empty sphere, the lamp of the pure expanse, the lamp of self-arising wisdom) or six. Doctrinal anatomy; the practices using them are restricted.

term: ka ti shel gyi sbu gu can

definitions.definition: The crystal kati channel: the subtle channel linking the heart, seat of wisdom, to the eyes.
The heart (citta) as the 'precious palace' where wisdom and the peaceful deities abide in the body.
Samantabhadra, the primordial buddha, the dharmakāya; also the name of the nature of mind itself.
'The all-good': the variety appearing as Vairocana, the all-good (Kunjed Gyalpo ch.31).
Kuntu Zangpo, the Bön-body (bon sku), primordial buddha of Bön.

term: rang bzhin rdzogs pa chen po

definitions.definition: The natural Great Perfection: the nature of mind as already perfect, the object of Dudjom Lingpa's 'Buddhahood Without Meditation'.
The teaching, reality and religion of Tönpa Shenrab — the word Bön uses as Buddhists use 'chos' (dharma); 'bon nyid' is reality itself.
The swastika (left-turning in Bön), emblem of the eternal and indestructible; 'Yungdrung Bön' is 'eternal Bön'.
The Bön-body, Bön's equivalent of the dharmakāya, personified as Kuntu Zangpo; with the body of perfection (rdzogs sku, Shenlha Ökar) and the emanation body (sprul sku, Tönpa Shenrab).

equivalents.note: the first of the three bodies in each system

definitions.definition: Priest or practitioner of Bön; also names the ways (theg pa) of the nine (phywa gshen, snang gshen...) and Tönpa Shenrab's clan.
The vital principle or 'soul' that can wander or be stolen, restored by the la-gug (bla 'gugs) rite; shared with Nyingma ritual practice.
Used in Nyingma life-force rituals (bla 'gugs, tshe 'gugs) shared with Tibetan religion generally.
Smoke purification offering of fragrant juniper and substances to deities, protectors and local spirits (Nyingma treasure liturgies, e.g. the Riwo Sangchö).
Bön smoke purification offering, among the rites of the causal ways.
'Mother and son': the base (mother) and awareness (son) recognized as inseparable; the meeting of mother and son clear light at death.
Mother and child luminosity: the ground luminosity at death and the path luminosity recognized in practice, whose meeting is liberation.
In the mind series, bodhicitta (byang chub kyi sems) is the primordial nature itself, the 'all-creating king': 'byang' purified, 'chub' all-pervading, 'sems' the unceasing all-maker.
In Mahāyoga, the ultimate and relative bodhicitta generated as wisdom (Guhyagarbha ch.2); in the preliminaries, the aspiring and applying mind of awakening.
The dharma-body, personified as Samantabhadra; in Dzogchen the ground recognized, empty essence.
The enjoyment body: the five buddha families and the peaceful and wrathful deities in Akaniṣṭha; in the Kunjed Gyalpo the retinues of earth, water, fire, wind and space.
The emanation body: the six sages of the six realms who teach the vehicles (Guhyagarbha ch.3), Garab Dorje, Śākyamuni and Padmasambhava.
Reality (chos nyid); in the four visions the 'direct perception of dharmatā' and the 'exhaustion of phenomena in dharmatā'; the bardo of dharmatā after death.
The expanse of reality (chos dbyings), in which all phenomena arise as display — the theme of Longchenpa's Chöying Dzöd.

The sugata-essence (bde gshegs snying po): in the Guhyagarbha the source from which conceptual karma emanates the realms; for Mipham the union of luminosity and emptiness with qualities spontaneously present.

cross_language.form: de bzhin gshegs pa'i snying po

definitions.definition: Primordial wisdom (ye shes), distinguished from dualistic consciousness (rnam shes); five wisdoms of the five families; 'self-arising wisdom' in Dzogchen.
Essence or sphere (thig le): the drops of the subtle body in the completion stage; in Dzogchen the single sphere (thig le nyag gcig) of reality and the spheres of light of the visions.

Channel (rtsa): the central channel (dbu ma) with the right (ro ma) and left (rkyang ma) channels and the wheels at the crown, throat, heart and navel, worked with in Anuyoga completion; in Dzogchen also the kati channel.
Wind (rlung): the five root and five branch winds that move in the channels; karmic winds of delusion and wisdom winds, mastered in the completion stage.
The lama (bla ma), root of blessings and the first of the three roots, to be examined before and followed after accepting; visualized as Padmasambhava in guru yoga.

Sacred commitment (dam tshig) binding disciple, teacher and deity, kept by the tantric practitioner; in Dzogchen, the four samayas of non-existence, evenness, spontaneous presence and singularity; the Kunjed Gyalpo even speaks of 'samaya with nothing to guard'.
Empowerment (dbang): the vase, secret, wisdom and word empowerments (also received symbolically in guru yoga); in Dzogchen, the empowerment of awareness's expressive power.
The maṇḍala (dkyil 'khor) of deities which the Guhyagarbha declares to be the primordial nature of appearances; also the maṇḍala offering of the preliminaries.
Continuum (rgyud): the ground continuum (buddha-nature), path continuum and fruit continuum; also the scriptures of the secret mantra, in the Nyingma arranged as the six tantra-vehicles.
Sky-goer (mkha' 'gro ma): female wisdom beings; the third root; keepers and entrusters of treasures; Yeshe Tsogyal as the queen of ḍākinīs.
The wrathful, blood-drinking forms of the buddhas (khrag 'thung), such as the Eight Herukas of the Kagye and the wrathful deities of the bardo.

Awareness-holder (rig 'dzin): an accomplished tantric master; in Mahāyoga the four levels of vidyādhara (matured, mastery over life, mahāmudrā, spontaneous presence); also the eight Indian vidyādharas of the Kagye transmission.
In Mahāyoga the third vidyādhara level (the mahāmudrā vidyādhara, body as the deity's form); the 'great seal' of the deity in generation-stage practice.
